text: The passenger pigeon was once probably the most common bird in North America, with perhaps 3 to 5 billion of them in the early 1800s. Flocks were so huge they darkened the sky for hours. Yet by 1900 almost none were left in the wild, and on 1 September 1914 the very last one, named Martha, died in a zoo in Cincinnati, Ohio.

They were wiped out mainly by people. Hunters killed them in staggering numbers to sell as cheap meat, and the forests they needed were cut down for farms. Because passenger pigeons only bred well in giant groups, once their numbers fell, they couldn't recover.

sec.t:
People who saw the flocks struggled to describe them. In 1813 the bird artist John James Audubon watched pigeons pass over Kentucky for three days, so thick they blocked out the midday Sun.

In 1866 a flock flew over southern Ontario in Canada that witnesses said was about 1.5 kilometres wide and 500 kilometres long. It took around 14 hours to pass. Some estimates put it at over three billion birds, though nobody could really count.

The birds were sleek and long-tailed, bigger than the [[@pigeons-homing|pigeons]] in city squares, with a rosy chest. Their name comes from the French word *passager*, meaning passing by.

In the 1800s, the [[@telegraph|telegraph]] let hunters learn within hours where a new colony had formed. Railways then carried them there, along with barrels and ice. Professional hunters netted and shot birds by the thousands and shipped them by train to cities like New York and Chicago, where pigeon pie was cheap food.

At the same time, settlers cleared the eastern forests for farmland. Fewer trees meant less food. Colonies became smaller, and small colonies failed. By the 1890s, flocks had nearly vanished. The last confirmed wild passenger pigeon was shot by a boy in Ohio in 1900.

A few birds lived on in zoos. The last of them was Martha, named after Martha Washington, wife of the first US president. She lived at the Cincinnati Zoo, where visitors came to see the final passenger pigeon. She died in 1914, aged about 29.

Her body was frozen in a block of ice and sent by train to the [[@smithsonian|Smithsonian]] in Washington, where she's kept to this day. In 2014, a hundred years after her death, the museum put her on display again in an exhibition about lost birds.

The pigeon's fall shocked many Americans and helped change the law. In 1900 the USA passed the Lacey Act, one of its first national laws to protect wildlife. Later laws protected [[migration|migrating]] birds.

Today, some scientists are studying the passenger pigeon's DNA, from museum specimens, and hope one day to recreate a similar bird using its living relative, the band-tailed pigeon. Whether that's possible, or wise, is one of the big debates around [[@lost-de-extinction|de-extinction]]. And the strangest part? Australia lost its striped [[@lost-thylacine|Tasmanian tiger]] only 22 years after Martha died, for many of the same reasons.

text: The driest place on Earth that isn't covered in ice is the Atacama Desert in northern Chile, a long strip squeezed between the Pacific Ocean and the Andes mountains. The coastal city of Arica averages less than 1 mm of rain a year. That is less rain in a whole year than Mumbai can get in a minute during a heavy [[monsoon|monsoon]] downpour.

If you count the polar regions, the driest spots are the McMurdo Dry Valleys of [[@antarctica|Antarctica]]. These valleys get almost no rain or snow, and fierce winds sweep away what little falls. Some scientists think parts of them have stayed dry for millions of years.

sec.h: Why the Atacama is so dry
sec.t:
Three things work together. First, the Andes block rain clouds from the Amazon side, creating a rain shadow. Second, a cold ocean current runs up the coast, cooling the air above the sea so it cannot rise to form rain clouds. Third, a zone of high pressure sits overhead, pressing down on the air and keeping skies clear.

The result is a land of salt flats, gravel and bare red hills. In the driest parts, scientists have found soil where almost no living things survive, even [[bacteria|bacteria]]. Abandoned mining towns and old machines decay very slowly, because there is so little moisture to rot or corrode them.

The dryness preserves things. About 7,000 years ago, the Chinchorro people of the Atacama coast began mummifying their dead. They removed organs, rebuilt bodies with sticks and plant fibres, and covered them in clay masks painted black or red. That is about 2,000 years before the Egyptians began making [[@mummies|mummies]].

Scientists think the Chinchorro may have started mummifying partly because the desert itself dried bodies naturally, and people saw the dead stay recognisable for years. In 2021, UNESCO made the Chinchorro sites a World Heritage Site.

Every few years, often during [[@el-nino|El Niño]], warm Pacific water brings a little extra rain. Within weeks, seeds that have waited in the soil for years sprout. Pink, purple and yellow flowers carpet the desert in what Chileans call the desierto florido, the flowering desert.

Some towns on the coast collect water from fog. Fine nets strung on hillsides catch droplets from sea mists called camanchaca, which drip into pipes and tanks below.

India's driest regions are the Thar Desert in Rajasthan and the cold deserts of [[@ladakh|Ladakh]], where parts get less than 100 mm a year. In Leh, much of the water comes from melting snow and [[glacier|glaciers]], not rain. Even so, Ladakh gets far more than the Atacama.

Then there is the largest desert of all. Antarctica gets so little snowfall that, even though it is covered in ice, it counts as a desert. It covers about 14 million square km, bigger than the Sahara or any other [[@deserts-sand|hot, sandy desert]]. Its ice built up slowly, a thin dusting at a time, over hundreds of thousands of years.

myth: The inside of the Earth is a giant ball of liquid lava.

Most of Earth's inside is solid. The mantle is solid rock that flows very slowly, like extremely stiff toffee. Only the outer core is fully liquid, and it's metal, not lava. Magma forms in small pockets near the surface.

sec.t:
Earth is built in layers, a bit like a mango with its skin, flesh and stone, but with two parts to the stone.

The [[@earth-layers-crust|crust]] is the thin rocky skin we live on. It's 5 to 10 km thick under the oceans and up to about 70 km under big mountains like the Himalayas. Below it is the mantle, nearly 2,900 km of hot rock. It is solid, but it creeps slowly over millions of years, carrying the plates with it.

Next comes the outer core, a layer of liquid iron and nickel about 2,200 km thick. Its swirling makes Earth's [[@earth-magnet|magnetic field]]. At the very centre is the inner core, a solid ball of iron and nickel about 2,400 km across. That's about two-thirds the width of the Moon.

When a big earthquake strikes, its waves travel through the whole planet. Seismometers around the world time their arrival. Some waves, called P waves, can pass through both solids and liquids. Others, called S waves, can only travel through solids.

Scientists noticed that S waves never reach the far side of Earth from an [[@earthquakes|earthquake]]. Something in the middle blocks them. It must be liquid. That's how they found the outer core.

In 1936, a Danish scientist named Inge Lehmann spotted faint P waves arriving where none should be. She worked out that they were bouncing off something solid inside the liquid core. She had discovered the inner core, working from paper records of earthquake waves collected at stations around the world. She kept working on Earth's insides for decades and lived to be 104.

{{story:tunnels}}

People have tried to dig down. In the 1970s, scientists in the Soviet Union began drilling the [[@extreme-deepest-hole|Kola Superdeep Borehole]] near the Arctic. After about 20 years, they reached 12,262 m, the deepest artificial hole in the world. The hole is only about 23 cm wide, narrower than a dinner plate.

They had to stop because it was getting too hot, about 180 °C at the bottom. Even so, the hole barely scratched the crust. The deepest mines, in South Africa, go about 4 km down. Digging [[@tunnels|tunnels]] through mountains is hard enough.

Earth is still holding heat from when it formed, when rocks crashed together and melted. While the young planet was largely molten, heavy iron sank to the middle to form the core, and lighter rock floated up. A giant crash with another young planet, which probably also made the [[@moon-formed|Moon]], added even more heat. Some of the heat comes from [[@half-life|radioactive atoms]] deep inside, which give off energy as they slowly change.

The pressure is enormous too. At the centre, it is more than three million times the air pressure at the surface. That pressure squeezes the iron of the inner core so hard that it stays solid, even though it's as hot as the surface of [[@sun-what|the Sun]].

That inner heat drives almost everything that shapes our planet's surface. It powers volcanoes and [[@geysers-hot-springs|hot springs]], moves the plates, and builds mountains.

text: A thunderstorm needs three things: warm, damp air near the ground, something to push that air upwards, and an [[atmosphere|atmosphere]] where rising air keeps on rising.

On a hot afternoon, the Sun warms the ground, and the ground warms the air above it. Warm air is lighter, so it rises. As it climbs, it cools, and the water vapour in it turns into tiny droplets, forming a cloud. Turning vapour into water releases heat, which makes the air rise even faster.

Soon a small puffy cloud has grown into a towering cumulonimbus, often 12 km tall or more, with a flat top like an anvil. Inside, ice and water crash around, building up electric charge until [[@lightning|lightning]] flashes and thunder booms.

st.prompt: You see a lightning flash and count 9 seconds before you hear thunder. Roughly how far away was it?
st.reveal: Light reaches you almost instantly, but sound travels about 1 km every 3 seconds. Nine seconds means the lightning was about 3 km away, close enough to go indoors.

sec.t:
Most thunderstorms last less than an hour and go through three stages.

In the growing stage, warm air shoots upward in a strong current called an updraft. The cloud builds higher and higher, but there's little or no rain yet.

In the mature stage, raindrops and hailstones get too heavy for the updraft to hold. They fall, dragging cold air down with them in a downdraft. This is when the storm is at its fiercest, with heavy rain, gusty winds, lightning and sometimes [[@hailstorms-india|hail]].

In the dying stage, the downdraft takes over and cuts off the supply of warm air. The rain eases, and the tall cloud slowly falls apart. Some storms join up into long lines, called squall lines, that can march across hundreds of kilometres.

sec.h: Storms in India and the USA
sec.t:
In India, thunderstorms are common in the hot months just before the [[monsoon|monsoon]]. In Bengal, Odisha and Assam, sudden April and May storms called *kalbaishakhi*, or nor'westers, sweep in from the north-west in the late afternoon. They cool the air, bring rain and sometimes flatten crops.

In the USA, Florida has more thunderstorm days than any other state. On the Great Plains, special rotating thunderstorms called supercells can spin up [[@tornadoes|tornadoes]].

Lightning is one of the biggest weather dangers in India. The National Crime Records Bureau counted about 2,900 lightning deaths in 2022, many of them farmers working in open fields.

Weather experts have a simple rule: "When thunder roars, go indoors." If you can hear thunder, you're close enough to be struck. A solid building or a car with a metal roof is safe. Trees, open fields, beaches and water are not.

If you're caught outside, don't shelter under a lone tree. Stay away from metal fences and poles. Once indoors, avoid baths, showers and taps during the storm, since lightning can travel along pipes. Wait about 30 minutes after the last thunder before going out again.

Satellites now spot thunderstorms as they grow, and lightning [[sensor|sensors]] pick up flashes across whole countries. In India, the India Meteorological Department sends lightning warnings, and the government's Damini app shows strikes nearby. Forecasters can't say exactly where a bolt will land, but they can tell when the sky is getting ready to build one.

text: Yes. In 2022, NASA proved it by crashing a spacecraft called [[@space-asteroid-defence|DART]] into a small asteroid named Dimorphos. The crash changed Dimorphos's [[orbit|orbit]]. Its trip around its bigger partner got about 32 minutes shorter.
The trick is time. A tiny push given years before a possible collision adds up. By the time the asteroid reaches Earth's path, it can be thousands of kilometres off course, and miss us completely.

sec.t:
DART stands for Double Asteroid Redirection Test. Its target was a pair of [[asteroid|asteroids]]. The bigger one, Didymos, is about 780 m wide. Dimorphos, about 160 m wide, circles it like a small moon. That is roughly the length of one and a half football fields.

DART's final pictures suggest Dimorphos is a loose pile of boulders and rubble, held together by its own weak [[gravity|gravity]], rather than one solid rock.

Neither asteroid was ever a threat to Earth, and the test could not change that. NASA chose a pair on purpose. A tiny change in an orbit around the Sun would be very hard to measure. A change in how long a little moon takes to circle its partner can be timed from Earth with [[@telescopes-how|telescopes]].

Telescopes around the world, and the [[@hubble|Hubble]] and Webb space telescopes, watched the cloud of dust and rock that sprayed out. Hubble saw it stretch into a tail thousands of kilometres long, like a comet's.

That flying rubble mattered. As it blasted off, it pushed Dimorphos back like the exhaust of a rocket, so the asteroid got several times more push than the spacecraft alone could give. NASA had hoped to change the orbit by at least 73 seconds. The real change was about 32 minutes.

Dimorphos's speed changed by only a few millimetres per second, about the pace of a crawling snail. Over years, that is plenty.

About 66 million years ago, an asteroid around 10 km wide hit what is now Mexico. It helped wipe out the [[@extinction|dinosaurs]] and most other life on Earth. Rocks that big are rare, and none known is heading for us. Smaller ones, the size of Dimorphos, could still badly damage a city. In 2013, a rock only about 20 m wide exploded high above the city of Chelyabinsk in Russia. Its shock wave shattered windows across the city and injured more than a thousand people, mostly from flying glass.

[[astronomer|Astronomers]] search the sky every night for asteroids and track their orbits years ahead. If they ever find one on a collision course, DART shows that a well-aimed push could work.

Nobody has yet seen the [[crater|crater]] DART left. The European Space Agency launched a spacecraft called Hera in 2024 to visit the pair, measure Dimorphos's mass and study the damage close up. Its findings will help turn one successful experiment into a plan the whole world could use.

text: An eagle sees far because its eyes are huge for its size and built for detail. A golden eagle weighs about as much as a small cat, yet its eyeballs are close to the size of a grown-up's. Bigger eyes throw a bigger picture onto the back of the eye, so there is more room for detail.

The back of the eye, the [[retina|retina]], is also packed far more tightly with light-sensing cells than ours. Where you have one sharp spot in each eye, an eagle has two. Together these let it pick out a hare moving across a hillside long before the hare notices anything above.

sec.t:
From the outside you see only a small, fierce circle of an eagle's eye. Most of the eyeball is hidden inside the head, and it is not a neat ball. It is slightly stretched from front to back, partway between a ball and a short tube. The two eyes fill a large part of the skull.

That size comes at a price. The eyes can hardly move in their sockets. An eagle that wants to look sideways must turn its whole head, which is why birds of prey make those sudden, jerky glances. A bony ridge above each eye works like the peak of a cap, shading the eye from the glare of the sun.

sec.h: Two sharp spots in each eye

sec.t:
Popular books often say an eagle sees four to eight times better than you, and can spot a rabbit from 3 km away. Scientists who have actually tested eagles are more careful. In the 1980s, a researcher in Australia trained a wedge-tailed eagle to fly towards one of two screens with fine stripes. The bird could tell stripes apart when they were about twice as fine as the best human could manage.

Twice as sharp is still enormous. It means an eagle could read a car's number plate from roughly twice as far as the sharpest-eyed person you know. Other eagles may do even better, but few have been tested.

Seeing far is only half the job. An eagle must also keep its target in focus while it dives. A golden eagle can drop at well over 200 km/h, and its eyes keep adjusting as the ground rushes up. A see-through third eyelid sweeps across each eye to clean it and protect it during the strike.

In India, you can watch this skill in steppe eagles that arrive every winter, and in crested serpent eagles that watch from treetops for snakes. In the United States, the [[@bald-eagle|bald eagle]] does much of its hunting over water. It spots a fish under the ripples before it folds its wings and drops.

text: Jet streams are narrow bands of very fast wind, high in the sky, that wind their way around the planet. They blow roughly 9 to 16 km up, near the height where passenger jets fly, often at 150 to 300 km/h and sometimes faster.

They form where cold air from the poles meets warm air from the tropics. The big difference in temperature creates strong winds high up. Earth's spin then bends those winds so they blow mostly from west to east. There are two main jet streams in each half of the world: a polar jet and a subtropical jet.

st.reveal: Jet streams over the North Atlantic usually blow from west to east. Planes flying east ride the wind like a tailwind, and planes flying west battle against it. Eastward flights are often an hour or more quicker.

myth: Jet streams are made by jet planes.

Jet streams are natural winds, named because they are narrow, fast streams of air, like a jet of water from a hose. They were blowing long before planes existed. Pilots simply use them, or avoid them.
facts: two in each hemisphere, the polar and subtropical jets

sec.t:
Jet streams are not straight lines. They snake around the globe in great loops and waves, a few hundred kilometres wide but only a few kilometres deep. They shift north and south with the [[@seasons-why|seasons]] and from week to week.

Their path matters for weather. Storms and rain systems tend to form and travel along them. When the jet stream loops far south, it can drag icy polar air with it. When it loops north, warm air follows. If a loop gets stuck in one place, the same weather can sit over a region for days, bringing [[@heatwaves|heat waves]] or floods.

Airlines plan routes around jet streams every day. Flying east across the North Atlantic, planes ride the wind as a tailwind. Flying west, they avoid its strongest part. That's why a flight from New York to London is usually shorter than the trip back.

In February 2020, during a powerful winter storm, a British Airways jumbo jet caught an unusually fast jet stream. It flew from New York to London in 4 hours and 56 minutes, more than an hour faster than normal, a record for a regular passenger jet.

Balloonists use jet streams too. In 1999, the first nonstop [[@hot-air-balloons|balloon flight around the world]] rode them for much of its journey.

In winter, a subtropical jet stream flows over northern India and the Himalaya. It steers weather systems called western disturbances, which bring winter rain to the plains and snow to the mountains.

As summer comes, this jet shifts north of the Himalaya and the Tibetan Plateau. That shift is one of the signals that the [[@monsoon|monsoon]] is ready to arrive. During the [[monsoon|monsoon]], a different jet appears, blowing from the east, high above southern India. Weather scientists at the India Meteorological Department watch both closely.

The jet streams are driven by the temperature difference between the poles and the tropics. The Arctic is warming faster than most of the planet, which shrinks that difference.

Some scientists think this is making the polar jet stream slower and wavier, so weather gets stuck more often. Others say the evidence is not yet clear. Computers that make [[@weather-forecasts|weather forecasts]] and track [[@climate-change|climate change]] are helping to test both ideas.

text: A kaleidoscope is a tube with mirrors inside, usually two or three long strips joined into a narrow triangle. At one end is a small chamber of loose coloured beads, glass chips or bits of plastic. At the other end is a peephole.

When you look in, you see the beads directly in one small triangle. You also see their reflections in the mirrors, and reflections of those reflections, bouncing back and forth. Each copy is a flipped version of its neighbour, so together they make a pattern that is perfectly balanced around the centre, like a flower or a star.
Turn the tube and the beads tumble into new positions. Every reflection changes at the same moment, and a new pattern appears.

st.prompt: You stand two small mirrors on a table, joined at one edge with tape, and open them to 60 degrees. You put a coin between them. How many coins do you see in total?
st.reveal: Divide 360 by the angle between the mirrors. 360 ÷ 60 = 6, so you see the real coin and five reflections, arranged in a circle. Close the mirrors to 45 degrees and you'll see eight.

d.try: Tape two small mirrors together along one edge like a book. Stand them up and put a bead, a leaf or a scrap of coloured paper between them. Slowly open and close the "book" and count the copies. Find the angle that makes a pattern like a rangoli.
myth: A mirror reflects all the light that hits it.
Every ordinary mirror absorbs a little light with each reflection. That's why, in a kaleidoscope, the copies furthest from the centre look slightly darker, because their light has bounced more times.
facts: two or three mirrors joined in a long triangle
360 divided by the mirror angle gives the number of slices

sec.t:
Stand in front of one mirror and you see one reflection. Stand between two mirrors facing each other, as in some lifts or hairdressers' shops, and you see a long line of copies stretching away. Each [[@mirrors|mirror]] reflects what the other shows.

When two mirrors meet at an angle, the copies arrange themselves in a circle instead of a line. The angle decides how many. Divide 360 degrees by the angle between the mirrors. At 90 degrees you get four slices, at 60 degrees six, at 45 degrees eight. Kaleidoscope makers choose angles that divide 360 neatly, so the copies join up without a messy seam.

The kaleidoscope was invented in 1816 by David Brewster, a Scottish scientist who studied how light reflects and bends. He was experimenting with mirrors and noticed the beautiful patterns. He named his invention from three Greek words: *kalos*, beautiful, *eidos*, shape, and *skopeo*, to look.

He patented it in 1817, but a mistake meant other makers could copy it, and they did. Kaleidoscopes became a craze in Britain and across Europe and America, with huge numbers sold in a few months. Brewster himself earned very little from them. He became famous anyway, for his scientific work on light.

Look carefully at a kaleidoscope pattern. The copies near the centre are bright, but the ones near the outside are a little dimmer. That's because ordinary mirrors aren't perfect. Each time light bounces, a small amount is absorbed by the mirror.

The light that makes the outer copies has bounced many times, losing a little at each bounce. Expensive kaleidoscopes use specially coated mirrors that reflect almost all the light, so the pattern stays bright right to the edge.

Today artists build giant walk-in kaleidoscopes, and designers use the idea to make fabric prints and phone wallpaper. The [[@toys-history|toy]] itself has hardly changed in 200 years.

text: Air flowing past the ball behaves differently on the shiny side and the rough, seamed side.
That difference in airflow creates a sideways push, so the ball curves. A good swing bowler can make it move tens of centimetres in the air, enough to beat the edge of a bat.
Reverse swing was mastered by Pakistani fast bowlers in the 1980s and 1990s, and confused batters for years.

st.prompt: A new ball has one shiny side and one rough side, with the seam angled. Which way does it usually swing?
st.reveal: Usually towards the rough side (where the seam points). Air clings longer to the rough side, so it leaves the ball at different points on each side. That pushes the ball sideways. But with an old ball at high speed, it can do the opposite, called reverse swing!
st.nudge: Good guess! An old ball bowled very fast can do exactly that. It's called reverse swing.

Mehta R.D. (1985) Aerodynamics of sports balls. Annual Review of Fluid Mechanics 17.
n.certNote: The basic physics is well understood; scientists still debate some details of reverse swing.

d.try: Make a gully-cricket "tape ball" by wrapping electrical tape tightly around half of a tennis ball, leaving the other half fuzzy. Bowl it gently to a friend in an open space, holding the line between taped and fuzzy sides upright. Watch which way it moves. Many famous bowlers in South Asia first learned swing this way.
myth: Swing happens because the ball is spinning, like a curveball.
Conventional swing is not caused by spin. A swing bowler keeps the seam steady and tilted, and the difference in airflow on the two sides of the ball pushes it sideways. Spin is a separate trick.
facts: Pakistani fast bowlers, from the late 1970s

sec.t:
As a ball flies, a very thin layer of air, called the boundary layer, clings to its surface. At some point this layer peels away, leaving a messy wake behind the ball.

When the seam is tilted, it trips the air on one side into swirling, turbulent flow. Strangely, turbulent air clings to the ball for longer before peeling off. On the other, smoother side, the air peels off sooner. So the wake behind the ball is pushed to one side, and the ball is pushed the opposite way, towards the seam side. The same ideas about air clinging to curved surfaces help engineers design [[@airplanes-fly|aeroplane wings]].

With an old, scuffed ball bowled very fast, something odd happens. The air becomes turbulent on both sides, and the ball swings the opposite way, away from the seam and towards the shiny side. This is reverse swing.

It was developed by Pakistani bowlers such as Sarfraz Nawaz and Imran Khan, and perfected in the 1990s by Wasim Akram and Waqar Younis. They used it to bowl late-swinging yorkers at the batter's toes. Because it comes late in the ball's flight, it is very hard to play. Scientists still argue about exactly what speeds and ball conditions make it happen.

Many players believe cloudy, humid days help swing. Scientists have tested this, and the evidence is mixed. It's still being argued about. Some think the effect is real but small. Others think cloudy days simply arrive with other helpful conditions, or that bowlers remember the days it worked. In England, where cloud is common, swing bowlers have long had a reputation for thriving.

Swing bowlers hold the seam upright and tilted, and release the ball with a steady wrist. A small change in angle changes everything. Too fast, and an ordinary new ball swings less. Too slow, and the airflow never becomes turbulent enough on the seam side.

India has produced fine swing bowlers, from Kapil Dev in the 1980s to Zaheer Khan and Bhuvneshwar Kumar more recently. England's James Anderson took over 700 wickets in [[@test-cricket|Test cricket]], more than any other fast bowler. Like the [[@cricket-spin|spinners]], they turn a tiny change in airflow into a ball the batter never quite reaches.

text: The FIFA World Cup began in 1930 in Uruguay. Football's world body, FIFA, wanted a [[tournament|tournament]] open to professional players from every country. Only amateurs were allowed to play at the [[@olympics|Olympics]], and many of the best players were now paid. Its president, a Frenchman named Jules Rimet, pushed the idea for years.
Only 13 teams took part, and Uruguay won. Today the tournament is held every four years, and the 2026 edition had 48 teams, with qualifying matches involving over 200 countries.

st.prompt: In the first World Cup final in 1930, Uruguay and Argentina could not agree on which ball to use. What did they do?

options.t: Used Argentina's ball in the first half and Uruguay's in the second
Tossed a coin and used the winner's ball all game
Asked the referee to bring a ball from France

st.reveal: Each team wanted its own ball, so they used one per half. Argentina led 2–1 at half-time with their ball. With Uruguay's ball in the second half, Uruguay scored three times and won 4–2.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, World Cup (football).

d.try: Run a mini World Cup with friends or cousins. Draw up four "countries", play short matches where each side meets every other side once, and keep a points table with 3 points for a win and 1 for a draw. Work out who goes through to the final.
myth: Brazil keeps the original World Cup trophy.

Brazil was allowed to keep the first trophy, the Jules Rimet Trophy, after winning it a third time in 1970. It was stolen in Rio de Janeiro in 1983 and never found. Today's trophy is a different one, first used in 1974.

sec.t:
Uruguay was a small country with a big football reputation. It had won the Olympic football gold in 1924 and 1928. It also offered to pay the travel and hotel costs of visiting teams, and 1930 was the hundredth anniversary of its first [[constitution|constitution]].

The capital, Montevideo, built a new stadium for the event, named Estadio Centenario after the anniversary. It was not quite finished when the tournament began, so the first matches were played elsewhere in the city.

There were no long-distance passenger flights in 1930. Teams from Europe had to sail across the Atlantic, a trip of about two weeks. Most European football associations said no.

Only four went: France, Belgium, Romania and Yugoslavia. Several of them travelled on the same [[@floating-ships|ship]], training on deck as it crossed the ocean. The rest of the field came from the Americas, including the United States, which reached the semi-finals. Frenchman Lucien Laurent scored the first World Cup goal, against Mexico.

[[@pop-world-cup-trophy|The original gold trophy]], later named after Jules Rimet, had an eventful life. During the [[@world-war-two|Second World War]], an Italian football official is said to have hidden it in a shoebox under his bed to keep it from the occupying army. No World Cups were held in 1942 or 1946.

In 1966, months before England hosted the tournament, the trophy was stolen from an exhibition in London. A week later a black-and-white collie called Pickles sniffed it out under a garden hedge. Brazil won it for the third time in 1970 and kept it, but it was stolen again in 1983 and never recovered.

The World Cup grew from 13 teams to 16, then 24, then 32 in 1998. In 2026 the USA, [[@canada|Canada]] and [[@mexico|Mexico]] hosted the first 48-team World Cup, with 104 matches. Mexico became the first country to host the men's tournament three times, after 1970 and 1986.

The Women's World Cup began in 1991 in China, and the United States won the first title. Brazil has the most men's titles, five, while Italy and [[@germany|Germany]] have four each.

India has never played at a men's World Cup. It qualified for 1950 after other teams in its group withdrew, but did not travel to Brazil. Many Indian fans still wonder what might have happened if it had.

text: When an adult donates blood, a nurse puts a thin needle into a [[vein|vein]] in the arm. Blood flows down a tube into a sterile bag, which is gently rocked so it doesn't clot. In about ten minutes, the bag holds around 350 to 450 millilitres, roughly two cups. That is only about a tenth of the [[@blood|blood]] in an adult's body.

The donor then rests for a few minutes with a drink and a snack. Meanwhile, the bag goes to a laboratory, where it is tested, sorted into parts and stored. Within days it could be inside someone who has had an accident, an operation or a serious illness.

st.prompt: Donated blood is often split into parts. Which part can be frozen and kept for about a year?
st.reveal: Plasma can be frozen and stored for around a year. Red cells last about five to six weeks in a fridge, and platelets only about five days at room temperature, which is why blood banks always need fresh donors.

American Red Cross, Blood donation process.

d.try: Ask an adult whether they know their blood group, and make a family chart. You might find that some people share a group and some don't. If an adult in your family donates blood, ask what the donation centre was like and what snack they got afterwards.
myth: Donating blood makes you weak for a long time.
A healthy adult gives only about a tenth of their blood. Most people feel normal within a few hours, after a rest, a drink and a snack. The body refills the lost liquid within a day or two.
facts: about 350–450 ml, roughly a tenth of your blood
healthy people aged 18–65 who weigh at least 45 kg

sec.t:
Not everyone can donate. In India, donors must be between 18 and 65, weigh at least 45 kg and be in good health. In the United States, the Red Cross accepts some 16- and 17-year-olds with a parent's permission, depending on the state.

First, a health worker asks questions about recent illnesses, medicines and travel. Then they prick a finger to check [[haemoglobin|haemoglobin]], the iron-rich [[protein|protein]] that carries oxygen. If it is too low, the person is asked to come back another day. These checks protect the donor as much as the patient.

A full bag of blood is spun very fast in a machine called a centrifuge. The heavy red cells sink to the bottom. The yellow plasma floats on top, and a thin layer of [[platelet|platelets]] sits in between.

Each part helps a different patient. Red cells help someone who has lost a lot of blood. Platelets help blood clot, and are often needed by people being treated for cancer. Plasma helps patients with burns or bleeding problems. So one donation can help up to three people.

Red cells keep for about five to six weeks in a [[@refrigerator|fridge]]. Platelets last only about five days. Plasma can be frozen for around a year.

{{story:red-cross}}

Every donated bag is tested for [[infection|infections]] that can spread through blood, such as HIV, hepatitis B and C, and malaria. Any bag that fails is thrown away.

Blood also has to match. In 1901, the Austrian doctor Karl Landsteiner discovered that people have different [[@blood-groups|blood groups]], now called A, B, AB and O, each either positive or negative. Giving the wrong type can make a patient very ill. People with O negative blood are especially valued, because their red cells can usually be given to anyone in an emergency.

Right after giving blood, your [[@heart-beat|heart]] and blood vessels adjust and keep blood pressure steady. Drinking water helps. Within a day or two, the body has replaced the lost plasma by pulling in fluid.

Red cells take longer. Bone marrow speeds up its work, and after about four to eight weeks the count is back to normal. That is why there are rules about waiting. In India, men may donate every three months and women every four. In the United States, the usual gap is 56 days.

Blood can't be made in a factory, and it doesn't keep forever. Hospitals need a steady stream of donors every week. Shortages often come during holidays, exam seasons and heatwaves, when fewer people turn up.

India marks National Voluntary Blood Donation Day on 1 October, and the world celebrates World Blood Donor Day on 14 June, Landsteiner's birthday. Children can't give blood, but they can help at school blood drives, make posters, or remind the adults around them that ten minutes in a chair can save a stranger's life.

text: When you read, light from the page or screen enters your eyes. Your brain spots the shapes of letters, groups them into words, links each word to its sound and meaning, and builds the sentence into an idea. All this happens in a fraction of a second, again and again, for every word.
Scientists can now watch it happen using brain scanners. They have found that reading uses a network of brain areas, mostly on the left side, that work together like a relay team.

st.prompt: How do your eyes move when you read a line of text?

options.t: In quick jumps with short pauses
In one smooth slide from left to right
Letter by letter, stopping on each one

st.reveal: Your eyes jump about seven to nine letters at a time and pause for about a quarter of a second. You take in words during the pauses and often skip short words like "the" without noticing.

src: Stanislas Dehaene, Reading in the Brain (Viking, 2009).

myth: With speed reading, you can read 1,000 words a minute and understand everything.
Studies find that reading much faster than normal means understanding and remembering much less. Skimming is useful for finding things, but it isn't the same as reading.

sec.h: A brain that learned a new trick
sec.t:
Humans have been talking for perhaps a hundred thousand years or more. But [[@writing-began|writing began]] only about 5,000 years ago, in places such as Mesopotamia and Egypt. That is far too recent for [[evolution|evolution]] to have built a special reading part of the brain.

So how do we read? The French scientist Stanislas Dehaene calls it "neuronal recycling". A patch of the brain that once only helped us recognise faces, tools and animals gets retrained to recognise letters. When a child learns to read, this patch slowly becomes a letter expert.

It takes years. A beginner sounds out each letter, c-a-t, slowly joining sounds into a word. With practice the brain stops spelling things out and recognises whole familiar words at a glance. That is why a seven-year-old reads aloud haltingly while an older sibling races through a comic, and why daily practice matters so much in the early years.

Your [[@eyes-see|eyes]] don't scan smoothly. They make quick jumps called saccades, each about seven to nine letters long, then stop for about a quarter of a second. You only take in words during those stops. Short, common words like "a", "of" and "the" are often skipped completely.

Your brain glues these snapshots together so smoothly that reading feels continuous. A skilled adult reading silently manages about 200 to 300 words a minute.

Many people hear a quiet inner voice as they read. Brain scans show that silent reading still switches on some of the areas used for speech. That is why tongue-twisters can feel awkward even when you read them in your head.

Reading also builds pictures. When you read about a kick, areas linked to movement become a little more active. When a story describes a smell, smell areas may join in too. Good books feel real partly because your brain is quietly acting them out.

For some people, linking letters to sounds is much harder. This is called dyslexia, and by many estimates it affects roughly one person in ten to some degree. It has nothing to do with how clever someone is. Many scientists, artists and business leaders have dyslexia.

With the right teaching, people with dyslexia learn to read well. Some find audiobooks or special fonts helpful. People who are blind read with their fingers using [[@braille|Braille]], and brain scans show their visual areas still get involved, even though no light reaches them. It's one more sign of how flexible the [[@brain-works|brain]] is.

text: Ada Lovelace was an English mathematician who lived from 1815 to 1852. In 1843 she published a set of notes about the Analytical Engine, a mechanical computer designed by her friend [[@charles-babbage|Charles Babbage]].

One of those notes set out, step by step, how the machine could calculate a difficult series of numbers. Because it is a precise set of instructions for a computer, many people call it the first published computer program, and Lovelace the first programmer.
Historians still argue about how much of it was her own work. But her notes went further than Babbage's in one big way: she saw that a computer could work with more than numbers.

st.prompt: Ada Lovelace's famous program was designed to make the Analytical Engine calculate what?

options.t: A tricky series of numbers called Bernoulli numbers

st.reveal: In Note G, she set out, step by step, how the engine could work out Bernoulli numbers, a sequence used in advanced maths. It is often called the first published computer program, though the machine to run it was never built.

n.certNote: Historians disagree about how much of the famous 1843 notes was Ada Lovelace's own work and how much came from Charles Babbage, who had sketched some programs earlier. Most agree her vision of what computers could do was her own.

sec.h: A poet's daughter who loved maths
sec.t:
Ada was the only legitimate child of the poet Lord Byron. Her parents separated when she was a baby, and she never saw her father again. Her mother, Annabella Milbanke, was a keen mathematician and insisted that Ada study maths and science.

As a child, Ada designed a flying machine and studied birds' wings to work out how it might fly. She was often ill, but she kept learning. At 17, she met Charles Babbage at a party in London and saw a working part of his Difference Engine. She was gripped by it, and they became lifelong friends.

In 1842, an Italian engineer, Luigi Menabrea, wrote an article in French about Babbage's Analytical Engine. Lovelace translated it into English. At Babbage's suggestion, she added her own notes, labelled A to G. They ended up about three times longer than the article.

Note G includes a table showing how the engine could calculate Bernoulli numbers, a series used in higher maths. It sets out each operation and which parts of the engine would hold each number. It is an [[@algorithms|algorithm]] written for a machine.

Babbage had sketched some smaller programs before. Some historians think he deserves more credit for Note G; others say the notes show Lovelace's deep understanding. The argument continues.

{{story:women-maths}}

What stands out most is Lovelace's imagination. She wrote that the engine might work on things other than numbers, as long as they could be expressed as symbols. Musical notes, for example. She suggested it might one day compose elaborate pieces of music.

That is exactly what computers do now: they turn words, pictures and sounds into numbers and work with them. Lovelace called her way of thinking "poetical science", blending imagination and logic, perhaps a nod to the [[@poetry|poetry]] of the father she never knew.

She also wrote that the engine could only do what it was told. It could not, she said, come up with anything new by itself.

About a hundred years later, the computer pioneer [[@alan-turing|Alan Turing]] discussed this idea in a famous 1950 paper on whether machines could think. He called it "Lady Lovelace's objection" and argued against it. People still debate the question today, as computers write stories and [[@tech-ai-art|draw pictures]].

Lovelace died of cancer in 1852, aged 36, and was buried next to her father. For about a century, her notes were mostly forgotten.

When electronic computers arrived in the 1940s and 1950s, people rediscovered her work. In 1980, the US Department of Defense named a programming language Ada in her honour. Since 2009, Ada Lovelace Day, held each October, has celebrated women in science, technology, engineering and maths.

text: Homes got electricity in stages, over more than a century. First, scientists worked out how to make electric current with spinning magnets and coils of wire. Then inventors built practical [[@light-bulb|light bulbs]]. Finally, companies and governments built power stations and strung wires along streets, into houses, and out to villages and farms.

The first big public power station opened in New York in 1882. Rich city homes in America, Europe and India got electricity in the early 1900s. But it took many more decades to reach the countryside. In the United States, most farms were connected only in the 1940s and 1950s. In India, the last village was connected in 2018.

st.prompt: In 1882, what was electricity in homes mainly used for?
st.reveal: The first customers bought electricity almost only for electric light, to replace gas lamps and candles. Fans came soon after. Refrigerators, washing machines and radios arrived over the following decades as wiring spread.

myth: Benjamin Franklin discovered electricity by flying a kite in a storm.

People had studied electricity long before Franklin, making sparks by rubbing glass and amber. Franklin's famous kite experiment of 1752 was meant to show that lightning is a form of electricity. Historians still debate exactly how the experiment was done.

sec.t:
In 1831, the English scientist Michael Faraday found that moving a magnet near a coil of wire makes electricity flow in the wire. This is called [[@induction-stoves|electromagnetic induction]]. It sounds simple, but it is the basic idea behind almost every power station on Earth. Spin a magnet inside coils of wire, using steam, falling water or wind, and you get a flow of electric current.

For decades the discovery was mostly a lab experiment. People needed a reason to want electricity in their homes. That reason was light.

Calcutta saw a public demonstration of electric lighting in 1879. In 1897, India's first [[hydroelectric|hydroelectric]] power station opened at Sidrapong, near Darjeeling, using water rushing down the hills.

In 1902, a hydroelectric plant at Shivanasamudra, on the Kaveri river in [[@karnataka|Karnataka]], began sending power about 150 km to the Kolar Gold Fields. A few years later, in 1905, Bangalore became one of the first cities in Asia to light its streets with electric lamps. Today hydropower from [[@dams-power|dams]] still supplies part of India's electricity, alongside coal, solar, wind and [[@nuclear-power|nuclear power]].

Cities got electricity first because many customers lived close together. Villages and farms were spread out, so each kilometre of wire served few people.

In the United States, the government set up the Rural Electrification Administration in 1935. It lent money to farmers' groups to build their own power lines. Within about fifteen years, most American farms had electricity, along with electric pumps, milking machines and radios.

In India, after independence, the government spent decades building power lines to [[@villages-india|villages]]. On 28 April 2018, the government announced that Leisang, a small village in Manipur, had become the last inhabited village to be connected. A village counted as electrified once public buildings and at least 10 percent of homes had power. A later scheme called Saubhagya worked to connect the remaining homes.

Electricity changed daily life more than almost any other invention. It brought [[@ceiling-fans|fans]], pumps, [[@how-fridges-cold|refrigerators]] and lights to study by after dark.

text: Teleportation in the Star Trek sense, where you vanish here and appear there, is not possible today, and no one knows how to make it possible. But a real thing called quantum teleportation happens in laboratories all the time. It moves the information that describes a particle, not the particle itself.

In 2017, Chinese scientists used it to send the state of photons (particles of light) between a station in Tibet and a satellite called Micius, about 1,400 km apart. That is roughly the distance from Delhi to Mumbai. Three physicists, Alain Aspect, John Clauser and Anton Zeilinger, shared the 2022 Nobel Prize partly for the work that made this possible.

st.prompt: In real quantum teleportation, what actually travels from one place to another?

options.t: Information about a particle, which rebuilds it on a different particle at the far end
The particle itself, flying faster than light
A tiny copy, while the original stays exactly as it was

st.reveal: No matter moves. The state of one particle is recreated on another particle far away, and the original's state is destroyed in the process. It also needs an ordinary signal, so nothing beats the speed of light.

src: Nobel Prize Outreach, The Nobel Prize in Physics 2022 (Aspect, Clauser, Zeilinger).

n.certNote: Quantum teleportation of tiny particles is proven and repeated in labs. Teleporting a person breaks no known law outright, but most physicists think it is so far beyond any possible technology that it may never happen.

d.try: Play "fax teleporter" with a friend. Build a small shape from 10 Lego bricks, then describe it in words only, while your friend copies it out of sight. Count how many sentences you needed. Now think about describing every atom in a human body instead of 10 bricks.
myth: Quantum teleportation means scientists can already zap small objects from place to place.
Only the quantum state of particles such as photons and atoms has been teleported. Not a single grain of sand, let alone a cat, has ever been sent this way.

sec.t:
A person isn't one particle. An adult body has about 7 followed by 27 zeros of [[atom|atoms]]. If you listed each atom's type, position and movement, the description would dwarf every hard disk on Earth put together. Rough estimates suggest that sending it with today's technology would take longer than the universe has existed.

Then comes a creepier problem. Because the original state is destroyed, a teleporter would take you apart here and build someone new over there from fresh atoms. Would that person be you? Philosophers have argued about this for decades, and no experiment can settle it. Some call it the teleporter problem, and it turns up in classrooms as a favourite puzzle about what makes you, you.

sec.h: A transporter born from a budget
sec.t:
When Star Trek began on American television in 1966, showing a spaceship landing on a different planet each week needed costly models and effects. Beaming the crew down with a shimmer of light was quicker and cheaper. The idea became so famous that "Beam me up" is now an everyday joke, even though nobody in the original series said exactly those words.

[[@science-fiction|Science fiction]] has a habit of giving scientists ideas, which is a big part of the [[@star-wars-effect|Star Wars effect]] on real research.

There is a cheat that already works. In 2021, a NASA doctor and his team appeared as live 3D images aboard the International Space Station, using a camera system Microsoft calls "holoportation". The astronaut wore a headset and could see and talk to them as if they were floating in the cabin. No atoms moved, of course. The images were built from cameras on Earth and sent up as data, about 400 km to the station, in a few seconds. It is a very fancy version of a [[@tech-video-calls|video call]].

Quantum teleportation may never carry people, but it could carry secrets. Messages sent this way can't be copied without leaving a trace, which makes them a dream for [[@encryption|encryption]]. Scientists hope to link [[@quantum-computers|quantum computers]] in different cities into a quantum internet, and satellites like Micius are the first test runs.

So the honest answer is that we already teleport, just not the way films promised. And if you think moving through space is hard, physicists have even stranger ideas about moving through [[@future-time-travel|time]].

text: A supercomputer is a machine built to do enormous amounts of maths very quickly. It is used for problems too big for any normal computer: forecasting the [[@monsoon|monsoon]], designing aircraft, testing new medicines on screen and simulating how [[@galaxies|galaxies]] collide.

Speed is measured in FLOPS, or floating-point operations per second, which roughly means calculations with [[decimal|decimal]] numbers. The fastest machines now manage more than one exaflop: a billion billion calculations every second. In 2025, the fastest on the official world ranking, the TOP500 list, was El Capitan at the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in California.

st.prompt: An exaflop machine does a billion billion sums a second. If all 8 billion people on Earth did one sum a second, how long to match one second of its work?
st.reveal: A billion billion divided by 8 billion is 125 million seconds. That's about four years, with nobody stopping to sleep or eat.

d.try: Time yourself doing 20 simple additions, such as 37 + 48, on paper. Work out how many you can do in a second. Then divide 1,000,000,000,000,000,000 (one exaflop) by your answer to find how many of you it would take to match a supercomputer for one second.
myth: A supercomputer is one giant, super-powerful computer chip.
Modern supercomputers are thousands of ordinary-looking computers, called nodes, linked by very fast cables and working on pieces of the same problem at once. The speed comes from teamwork.
facts: more than 1 exaflop, a billion billion a second

sec.t:
An exaflop is 1 followed by 18 zeros. Suppose all 8 billion people on Earth each did one sum a second. Dividing a billion billion by 8 billion gives 125 million seconds. So it would take humanity about four years, without sleep, to match what the fastest machine does in one second.

All that work uses a lot of power. The biggest systems draw around 20 to 30 megawatts, as much as tens of thousands of homes. Much of that turns into heat, so many are cooled by water pumped through pipes beside the chips.

[[@weather-forecasts|Weather forecasting]] is one of the biggest jobs. The [[atmosphere|atmosphere]] is split into a 3D grid of boxes. For each box, the computer works out temperature, wind, pressure and moisture, then calculates how they will change a few minutes later, and repeats this again and again.

Smaller boxes mean better forecasts but far more sums. India's [[monsoon|monsoon]] is famously hard to predict, so the government built powerful weather machines. One called Pratyush, installed at the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology in Pune in 2018, was among the fastest in India. Better forecasts help farmers decide when to sow and give warning before [[@cyclones-india|cyclones]].

In the 1980s India wanted a supercomputer for weather work, but the United States, worried about military uses, refused to sell the most powerful kind. So in 1988 the government set up the Centre for Development of Advanced Computing, C-DAC, in [[@pune|Pune]]. Led by the computer scientist Vijay Bhatkar, its team built PARAM 8000 in 1991 by linking many smaller processors together, the same idea the world's fastest machines use today.

The PARAM family has grown ever since. Under the National Supercomputing Mission, dozens of PARAM systems now work in universities and labs across India.

Every June and November the TOP500 list ranks the world's fastest machines. The United States, China, Japan and countries in Europe compete for the top spots. In 2022 Frontier, at Oak Ridge in Tennessee, became the first machine on the list to pass one exaflop. Japan's Fugaku held the top place before it.

Engineers are now building machines for [[@ai-what|artificial intelligence]], which need huge numbers of simpler sums. Scientists also hope [[@quantum-computers|quantum computers]] might one day take on special problems that even an exaflop machine can't handle in a lifetime.

text: Edmund Hillary from [[@new-zealand|New Zealand]] and Tenzing Norgay, a [[@people-sherpas|Sherpa climber]] who lived in Darjeeling, India, were the first people known to stand on the summit of Mount Everest. They reached it at about 11:30 in the morning on 29 May 1953.

They were part of a British [[expedition|expedition]] led by John Hunt, with hundreds of porters and many climbers who carried supplies higher and higher up the mountain. Hillary and Tenzing spent about 15 minutes on top, took photographs and left small offerings in the snow. Then they climbed down. The news reached London on the morning of Queen Elizabeth II's coronation.

options.t: By calculating with angles measured from far away on the plains
By climbing it with a long tape measure
By flying over it in a balloon

st.reveal: Surveyors measured angles to the peak from stations more than 160 km away in India. The mathematician Radhanath Sikdar is often credited with doing the calculations that showed Peak XV was higher than any other known peak.

d.try: Climb a flight of stairs quickly and count your breaths in the next minute. Then rest and count again. At the top of Everest, each breath holds about a third of the oxygen it does at sea level, so climbers breathe hard even when standing still.
myth: The top of Everest is the farthest point on Earth from the planet's centre.
Because Earth bulges at the equator, the summit of Mount Chimborazo in Ecuador is farther from Earth's centre, even though Everest is highest above sea level.
facts: 8,848.86 m, measured by China and Nepal in 2020

sec.t:
In the 1800s, the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India measured the land with chains, telescopes and lots of maths. From the plains, surveyors measured angles to distant peaks of the [[@himalaya-form|Himalaya]], mountains still being pushed up as India presses into Asia.

In 1852, calculations showed that a mountain called Peak XV was the highest on Earth. The mathematician Radhanath Sikdar is often credited with the discovery. In 1865 the peak was named after George Everest, a former head of the survey, though he had objected. Local people already had their own names: Chomolungma in Tibetan and, later, Sagarmatha in Nepali.

British expeditions tried from Tibet in the 1920s and 1930s. In 1924, George Mallory and Andrew Irvine were last seen climbing high on the summit ridge before cloud hid them. They never came back. Mallory's body was found in 1999, but his camera was not. Nobody knows if they reached the top.

The 1953 team came from Nepal, which had recently opened to outsiders. They set up a chain of camps up the mountain. Climbers used bottled oxygen, heavy metal tanks they carried on their backs.

Above 8,000 m is the "death zone", where the air holds so little oxygen that the body slowly weakens. Your [[@lungs-breathe|lungs]] work harder and harder but cannot take in enough. A first summit team, Tom Bourdillon and Charles Evans, got within about 100 m of the top on 26 May before turning back.

Three days later, Hillary and Tenzing set off from a tiny tent at about 8,500 m. Near the top, they faced a steep rock step about 12 m high, now called the Hillary Step. Hillary wriggled up a crack beside it, and Tenzing followed. Soon after, there was nowhere higher to go.

In 1975 Junko Tabei of Japan became the first woman on top. In 1984 Bachendri Pal became the first Indian woman to reach the summit. Thousands of people have now climbed Everest, and in busy seasons there are queues near the top.

The mountain is still growing by a few millimetres each year as India's plate pushes into Asia. In 2020, China and [[@nepal|Nepal]] announced a new joint height of 8,848.86 m, measured using [[@satellites-help|satellites]] and a team that carried equipment to the summit.

text: The Mongols were nomadic herders from the grasslands, or steppe, of Mongolia. In 1206 a leader named Temujin united the Mongol tribes and took the title [[@genghis-khan|Genghis Khan]]. He and his sons and grandsons then conquered China, Central Asia, Persia, Russia and parts of Eastern Europe.

By the late 1200s the Mongol Empire covered about 23 to 24 million square kilometres, the largest connected land [[empire|empire]] in history. Their success came from expert horse archers, fast-moving armies organised in units of ten, ruthless use of fear, and a willingness to borrow skills from the peoples they conquered.

st.prompt: How many horses did a Mongol soldier usually take on campaign?

options.t: Several, so he could switch to a fresh one
Just one, which he rode the whole way
None, because Mongol soldiers mostly walked

st.reveal: Each warrior typically had several horses and changed mounts so none got too tired. That let Mongol armies cover distances that left their enemies astonished, sometimes well over 100 km in a day.

n.certNote: Historians agree the Mongol Empire was the largest connected land empire in history. Figures for its size and for the number of people killed in its wars are estimates, and some old chronicles exaggerated them.

d.try: Practise Mongol-style counting. Ask nine friends or family members to stand in a group of ten, with one as leader. Then imagine ten such groups making a hundred. Work out how many leaders a group of 10,000 would need at every level.
myth: The Mongols won only because they had huge numbers.
Mongol armies were often smaller than their enemies'. They won through speed, discipline, clever tactics, good spies and the skill of horse archers trained from childhood.

sec.t:
Mongol children learned to ride almost as soon as they could walk. Herding animals across the open steppe made them tough, patient and expert archers. Their bows, made of wood, horn and sinew glued together, were short enough to shoot from the saddle and powerful enough to fire arrows a long way.

Each soldier brought several horses and switched between them. Mongol armies could ride fast and far, live on dried meat and mare's milk, and appear where no one expected them.

The Mongol conquests were often terrifying. Cities that surrendered might be spared. Cities that resisted were often destroyed, and many of their people killed, so that the next city would give in without a fight.

In 1258 Mongol forces captured Baghdad, then one of the world's great centres of learning, and destroyed much of it. [[medieval|Medieval]] writers gave huge death tolls for these campaigns, some probably exaggerated, but historians agree that millions died across Asia and Europe.

Once in control, the Mongols kept the roads safe. They set up the *yam*, a network of relay stations with fresh horses and supplies, a little like a postal system. Officials carried a *paiza*, a metal tablet that worked like a passport.

During this "Mongol peace", merchants, missionaries and ideas moved along the [[@silk-road|Silk Road]] more easily than before. The Venetian traveller [[@marco-polo|Marco Polo]] spent years at the court of Kublai Khan, grandson of Genghis, who founded the Yuan [[dynasty|dynasty]] in China. [[@money-banks|Paper money]], gunpowder and printing ideas spread west, though disease may have travelled along the same routes.

Not every campaign succeeded. Kublai Khan's fleets tried to invade Japan in 1274 and 1281 and were wrecked by storms. The Japanese called the winds *kamikaze*, divine winds. In 1260, an army of the Mamluks of Egypt defeated the Mongols at Ain Jalut, in today's Israel.

India was also defended. The [[@delhi-sultanate|Delhi Sultanate]], especially under Alauddin Khilji around 1300, beat back several Mongol invasions. By the 1260s, the empire had split into four khanates ruled by different branches of the family. Two centuries later, a prince called Babur, descended from Genghis Khan, founded the Mughal Empire in India.

text: The Underground Railroad was a secret network of people and safe houses in the United States in the 1800s. It helped enslaved Black people escape from the Southern states, where slavery was legal, to the North and to Canada, where they could live free.

It was not underground, and it had no trains. The name was a kind of code. Guides were called conductors. Safe houses were stations. The people escaping were sometimes called passengers or cargo. Using railway words let helpers talk about it without giving it away.
Nobody knows exactly how many people it helped. Historians estimate somewhere between about 30,000 and 100,000.

st.prompt: Many people escaping slavery travelled at night. What did they often use to find north?

options.t: A pocket compass from the shop

st.reveal: The North Star, Polaris, stays almost still in the sky while the others turn around it. Many freedom seekers found it by following the two end stars of the Big Dipper, and walked towards it.

n.certNote: Because the network was secret, few records were kept. Estimates of how many people escaped through it range from about 30,000 to 100,000, and many stories about hidden tunnels and codes cannot be proved.

d.try: On a clear night, with an adult, look north and find the Big Dipper (in India it is called the Saptarishi). Follow the line made by its two end stars to a fairly bright star on its own. That is the North Star, which people escaping slavery used as a guide.
myth: Families sewed secret codes into quilts to show escaping people the way.

This idea became popular from a 1999 book, but historians have found no evidence from the time that quilt codes were used. The real network relied on word of mouth, songs, trusted helpers and the stars.

sec.t:
Some escapes needed more than walking. In 1849, Henry Brown, enslaved in Richmond, Virginia, had a friend nail him inside a wooden crate about the size of a small cupboard. It was labelled "dry goods" and sent by train and steamboat to Philadelphia.

The trip took 27 hours. At times the box was set down upside down, with Brown on his head. Anti-slavery workers finally pried open the lid. Brown reportedly climbed out and greeted them politely, as if he had just stepped off a train. He became known as Henry "Box" Brown, and toured Northern towns and later Britain telling his story, sometimes with a copy of the box on stage.

[[@harriet-tubman|Harriet Tubman]] escaped slavery in Maryland in 1849. Then she did something astonishing: she went back. Over about eleven years she returned roughly 13 times and guided about 70 people to freedom, including members of her own family.

She travelled in winter, when nights were long. She sometimes set off on Saturday nights, because notices about runaways could not appear in newspapers until Monday. She later said she "never lost a passenger".

In 1850, the US government passed the Fugitive Slave Act. It said that people who had escaped could be captured even in free Northern states and sent back. Anyone who helped them could be fined or jailed. Suddenly the North was not safe.

So many freedom seekers kept going, across the border into [[@canada|Canada]], where slavery had been abolished in 1834 under British law. Towns such as St Catharines in Ontario became new homes. Tubman herself lived there for several years.

Because the network was secret, few people wrote anything down at the time. One who did was William Still, a free Black man in Philadelphia. He interviewed hundreds of people who passed through, including Henry Brown, and published their stories in 1872.

The network grew quieter after the [[@us-civil-war|Civil War]], which ended slavery in the United States in 1865. Today the US National Park Service keeps a list of hundreds of real Underground Railroad sites. And one of the people who escaped slavery, Frederick Douglass, used his freedom to become one of the most powerful speakers in American history.

text: The Arctic is the region around the North Pole. At its heart is the Arctic Ocean, covered for much of the year by sea ice that freezes, cracks, drifts and melts with the seasons. Around it lie the northern edges of eight countries: Canada, the United States (through [[@alaska|Alaska]]), Russia, [[@norway-fjords|Norway]], Sweden, Finland, [[@iceland|Iceland]] and Denmark (through [[@world-greenland|Greenland]]).

Unlike Antarctica, the Arctic has people who have lived there for thousands of years. About 4 million people live in the Arctic today, in [[@people-fishing-villages|fishing villages]], mining towns and a few cities. Polar bears, walruses, arctic foxes, narwhals and reindeer share it with them.

d.try: Put an ice cube in a glass of water and mark the water level with a pen. Wait until the ice melts and check the level again. It barely changes, which is why melting floating sea ice raises the sea far less than melting ice on land.
myth: Polar bears hunt penguins.
They never meet. Polar bears live only in the Arctic, and wild penguins live almost only in the Southern Hemisphere, with Antarctica at the far end. Polar bears mostly hunt seals.
facts: the Arctic Ocean, mostly covered by floating ice
about 4 million live in the Arctic

sec.h: Months of light, months of dark

sec.t:
The Inuit live across Arctic Canada, Greenland and Alaska. The Sámi live in the north of Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia, and many have herded reindeer for generations. Siberia has many more peoples, such as the Nenets, who move with huge herds across the [[@tundra|tundra]].

Traditional Arctic life depended on knowing the ice. Hunters could read cracks, colours and the sound of ice underfoot to tell whether it would hold them. Inuit languages have many precise words for kinds of sea ice. Today most Arctic people use snowmobiles, phones and the internet, while keeping hunting, fishing and their languages alive.

The Arctic is warming much faster than the rest of the planet, by some measures three to four times faster. One reason is simple. White ice reflects sunlight. When it melts, the dark ocean beneath absorbs more heat, which melts more ice.

Summer sea ice now covers far less of the Arctic Ocean than it did in the 1980s. This is hard on polar bears, which hunt seals from the ice. For people, melting ice and thawing frozen ground can crack roads and houses, and wash away coastlines.

sec.h: India at the top of the world
sec.t:
In 2008 India opened its Arctic research station, Himadri, in a tiny international science village called Ny-Ålesund on [[@world-svalbard|Svalbard]]. Indian scientists there study [[@glaciers|glaciers]], the [[atmosphere|atmosphere]] and how Arctic changes might affect the Indian [[monsoon|monsoon]].

Svalbard has another famous building: the Global Seed Vault, cut deep into a frozen mountainside. It stores backup copies of seeds from crops all over the world, including India, in case disaster strikes a seed bank elsewhere.

Arctic nights have their own beauty. The [[@aurora|aurora]], or [[@solar-wind|northern lights]], ripples across the sky in green curtains when particles from the Sun strike the upper atmosphere.

And above the pole itself shines Polaris, the [[@north-star|North Star]]. From the North Pole it sits almost straight overhead, which is why sailors far to the south once used it to find north. From India it hangs low over the northern horizon, and the further south you go, the lower it sinks.

text: The Amazon is the largest [[tropical|tropical]] rainforest on Earth. It covers about 5.5 million square kilometres of South America, an area bigger than India and Pakistan put together. Most of it is in Brazil, but it spreads into eight other countries.

Through the middle runs the Amazon River and more than a thousand streams that feed it. The forest is warm and wet all year. Those two things together let an enormous number of living things grow, from trees taller than a ten-storey building to frogs smaller than your fingernail.

st.reveal: Brazil holds about 60% of the forest. The rest is spread over Peru, Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador, Bolivia, Guyana, Suriname and French Guiana, which is part of France.

d.try: Put a small plant in a pot, water it, and cover it loosely with a clear plastic bag tied around the pot. Leave it in a bright spot for a day. The drops that form inside the bag are water the leaves breathed out, which is how the Amazon helps make its own rain.
myth: The Amazon makes 20% of the oxygen we breathe.

Its plants make huge amounts of oxygen, but the forest's animals, fungi and rotting leaves use up nearly all of it. The Amazon matters hugely for rain, for wildlife and for storing carbon, but it is not the Earth's spare pair of lungs.
facts: carries about a fifth of all the river water reaching the oceans
about 1 in 10 of all known kinds of plants and animals

sec.t:
The Amazon River carries more water than any other river. Roughly a fifth of all the fresh water that rivers pour into the world's oceans comes out of its mouth. Whether it is also the longest river is still argued over, and you can read why in the article on the [[@rivers-longest|longest rivers]].

At Manaus, the dark, tea-coloured Rio Negro meets the pale, muddy Solimões. Their water differs in speed, temperature and how much it carries, so they run side by side for kilometres, black and brown, before blending. Every rainy season the rivers rise many metres and flood the forest. Fish swim among tree trunks and eat fallen fruit, and some help plant new trees by dropping the seeds.

About one in every ten known [[species|species]] lives in the Amazon. There are jaguars, [[@power-sloth|sloths]], pink river dolphins, poison dart frogs and the giant Victoria water lily, whose floating leaves can grow wider than a dining table. New kinds of plants and animals are still being found every year.

Hundreds of [[indigenous|indigenous]] groups live in the Amazon, some in villages that have barely changed for generations and a few who avoid contact with outsiders altogether. Their knowledge of plants has led to [[@medicine-how|medicines]] and foods used far beyond the forest. Brazil nuts, cocoa and the açaí berry all come from Amazon trees. Studies of satellite maps show that forest inside indigenous lands is often cleared far less than forest outside them.

Large parts of the Amazon have been cut down for cattle ranches, soya farms, roads and mining. Scientists estimate that close to a fifth of the original forest has already been cleared. When trees are burned, the carbon stored in them goes into the air, which links the forest to [[@climate-change|climate change]].

Some researchers worry that if too much forest disappears, the flying rivers will weaken and parts of the Amazon could dry into grassland. Brazil's [[@what-if-no-trees|deforestation]] rate has risen and fallen over the years with changes in laws and how strictly they are enforced. The forest also gets help from far away. Every year, dust blown across the Atlantic from the [[@sahara|Sahara]] settles on the Amazon and adds [[nutrient|nutrients]] to its thin soil.

text: Kerala is a narrow state squeezed between the Arabian Sea and the green Western Ghats mountains, on India's south-west tip. It is about 590 km long but in places only 35 km wide. That shape gives it beaches, mountains and a maze of [[lagoon|lagoons]] all within a few hours' drive.

What makes Kerala stand out is its mix. It has some of India's best health and education results, a long history of trade with the world, and Hindus, Muslims and Christians who have lived side by side for centuries. Its name is often linked to *kera*, the [[@malayalam|Malayalam]] word for coconut, and coconut palms are everywhere.

st.reveal: The India Meteorological Department says the monsoon usually covers the whole country by about 8 July. It spreads north from Kerala over five or six weeks, which is why Delhi waits far longer for rain than Kochi.

d.try: Keep a monsoon diary. Ask a relative or friend in another Indian city when the rain started this year where they live, and compare it with your town. Mark the dates on a map of India and see if the monsoon moved from south to north.
myth: The monsoon arrives everywhere in India on the same day.
It reaches Kerala first, usually around 1 June, and moves north and west over the following weeks. It normally covers the whole country only by early July.
facts: about 94%, the highest of any state

sec.t:
Every year, around 1 June, the southwest [[@monsoon|monsoon]] reaches Kerala before anywhere else in India. Clouds roll in from the sea and hit the Western Ghats, dropping heavy rain on the hills. The India Meteorological Department announces the date, and the whole country watches, because farmers everywhere depend on it.

All that rain feeds 44 rivers, thick forests, and tea and spice plantations on the hills. It also fills the backwaters.

Behind the beaches lies a network of lagoons, lakes, canals and rivers, called the backwaters. Fresh water from the hills meets salty water from the sea here. Vembanad, the biggest lake, and its connected [[wetland|wetlands]] cover more than 1,500 km². People live along the canals, travelling by boat to school and market, and farming rice in fields that lie below sea level.

Old rice barges called kettuvallams have been turned into houseboats for visitors. During the [[@india-wonder-onam-boat-race|snake boat races]], long boats with over 100 rowers each race to the beat of songs. The Nehru Trophy race has been held since 1952.

[[@kathakali|Kathakali]] dancers wear huge skirts and painted faces, green for heroes and red for fierce characters, and act out stories from the epics with tiny eye and hand movements. It is one of India's great [[@indian-classical-dance|classical dance]] forms, along with Kerala's graceful [[@kuchipudi-mohiniyattam|Mohiniyattam]]. [[@sport-kalaripayattu|Kalaripayattu]] is a martial art with kicks, leaps and stick fighting that is still taught in Kerala today.

The biggest festival is [[@onam-pongal|Onam]], the harvest festival, when families make flower carpets called pookalam and eat a feast called [[@south-indian-meals|sadya]], served on a banana leaf. A full sadya can have more than 20 dishes, from sambar and avial to sweet payasam, and there is a set order for where each one goes on the leaf.

In the 2011 [[@census|census]], about 94% of people in Kerala could read and write, the highest of any Indian state. Kerala also has long life expectancy. Many Keralites work in Gulf countries such as the UAE and Saudi Arabia and send money home, which has built houses and businesses across the state.

text: Thailand is a country in mainland Southeast Asia, shaped a little like an elephant's head with its trunk running south down the Malay Peninsula. It has about 7 crore people. Bangkok, the capital, sits on the Chao Phraya River near the sea. Thais call it Krung Thep, short for a ceremonial name so long, 168 letters in the Roman alphabet, that Guinness World Records lists it as the [[@words-longest|longest place name]] anywhere.

Thailand is known for golden Buddhist temples, spicy and sour food, beaches and islands, elephants, and kickboxing called Muay Thai. It is also the only country in Southeast Asia that was never ruled by a European power. It is a kingdom, with a king as head of state, though since 1932 the king has not ruled alone.
