sec.t:
In the 1800s, Britain ruled Burma and Malaya to the west and south, and France ruled Laos, Cambodia and [[@vietnam|Vietnam]] to the east. Siam, as Thailand was then called, sat in between.

Its kings, especially King Mongkut and his son King Chulalongkorn, kept the country independent with careful diplomacy. They modernised the army, schools and railways, and signed [[treaty|treaties]] with both powers. Siam did have to give up some border lands to Britain and France. But it kept its independence while almost all its neighbours became colonies, and stayed independent through the long age of [[empire|empires]] that ended with [[@decolonisation|decolonisation]] after 1945. In 1939 the country changed its name to Thailand, meaning "land of the free".

Most Thais are Buddhists. Saffron-robed monks walk the streets at dawn collecting food from families, who see giving as a way of making merit. Many Thai boys spend a short time as novice monks, sometimes just a few weeks, as a rite of passage. The [[@buddha|Buddha]] appears everywhere, from giant reclining statues to tiny shrines in shops.

The Asian elephant is Thailand's national animal. Elephants once hauled teak logs out of forests and carried kings into battle. Logging with elephants was banned in 1989. Many of the country's few thousand captive [[@elephants-talk|elephants]] now live in camps and [[sanctuary|sanctuaries]], and a few thousand more still live wild in national parks.

Thai cooks aim to balance four tastes in one meal: sour from lime and tamarind, sweet from palm sugar, salty from [[@food-science-umami|fish sauce]] and spicy from chillies. Tom yum is a hot and sour soup with lemongrass and prawns. Green curry gets its colour from fresh green chillies and herbs.

Chillies only arrived in Asia from the Americas in the 1500s, carried by Portuguese traders, yet Thai food is now famous for them. Thailand is also one of the world's biggest rice exporters, and its fragrant jasmine rice smells faintly of popcorn when it cooks.

text: The most famous detective of all is probably Sherlock Holmes, the sharp-eyed London detective created by Arthur Conan Doyle. Close behind come Agatha Christie's Hercule Poirot and Miss Marple. In India, readers love Byomkesh Bakshi and Feluda from Bengal.
Fictional detectives have a lot in common. They notice small things others miss. They ask odd questions. And at the end they gather everyone together and explain who did it, and how they knew.
Detective stories, also called mysteries or whodunits, are a puzzle the reader tries to solve alongside the hero. That game is a big part of the fun.

sec.t:
Many people call Edgar Allan Poe's "The Murders in the Rue Morgue" the first modern detective story. Poe, an American writer, published it in 1841. His detective, C. Auguste Dupin, solves a baffling crime in Paris by careful reasoning.

Dupin had a friend who told the story, and he loved to explain his thinking at the end. Later writers copied both ideas. Poe wrote only three Dupin stories, but he set the pattern for almost every fictional detective who followed.

In 1887 a young doctor named Arthur Conan Doyle published A Study in Scarlet. It introduced [[@sherlock-holmes|Sherlock Holmes]] and his friend Dr Watson, who share rooms at 221B Baker Street in London.

Holmes reasons from tiny details. On meeting Watson, he can tell he has just come back from Afghanistan, from his tanned face, his stiff arm and his soldierly manner. Conan Doyle based this habit partly on a real teacher of his, the Scottish [[surgeon|surgeon]] Joseph Bell, who could guess a patient's job from their hands.

Conan Doyle grew tired of Holmes and killed him off in 1893, sending him over a waterfall. Readers were so upset that he brought Holmes back. In all he wrote four novels and 56 short stories.

Bengal has a strong love of mysteries. In 1932 Sharadindu Bandyopadhyay wrote the first story about Byomkesh Bakshi, who called himself a "truth-seeker" rather than a detective. Byomkesh solves crimes in Kolkata with his friend Ajit, who tells the stories.

In 1965 [[@satyajit-ray-stories|Satyajit Ray]], the great film director, began writing about Feluda for Sandesh, a children's magazine his grandfather had started. Feluda is tall, smart and fond of [[@logic|logic]]. His young cousin Topshe narrates, and a writer of thrillers named Jatayu often tags along for comic relief.

Both detectives have been made into many films and TV series. Other Indian languages have their own detectives too, from Tamil and Hindi pulp novels to the TV detective Karamchand.

Many children start with detective stories written for them. In the USA, the Hardy Boys first appeared in 1927 and Nancy Drew in 1930, and both are still in print. In Britain and India, generations grew up on [[@enid-blyton|Enid Blyton]]'s Famous Five and Secret Seven, groups of children who solve mysteries in the holidays.

Real detectives rely more on science than on clever guesses, using fingerprints, cameras and [[@dna|DNA]]. But the heart of a mystery story hasn't changed since Poe: notice what others miss, and think it through.

text: For nearly 200 years, Britain controlled large parts of India, first through the [[@east-india-company|East India Company]] and then directly from 1858 to 1947. Tens of thousands of British soldiers, officials, teachers and their families lived in India. Some were born there.

Writers among them wrote about what they saw, and readers in Britain were hungry for stories of a land that seemed distant and exotic to them. Adventure, jungles, palaces and [[@india-wonder-hill-stations|hill stations]] all made exciting reading. India also gave these writers material that no one in London had: new landscapes, languages, foods and people.
The best known is Rudyard Kipling, born in Bombay in 1865. Others include E. M. Forster, George Orwell and the hunter-writer Jim Corbett.

st.prompt: Kipling's novel Kim opens with a boy sitting on a giant old cannon outside a museum. Which city is it in?
st.reveal: Kim begins on Zamzama, a huge bronze gun outside the Lahore Museum, now in Pakistan. Kipling's father, John Lockwood Kipling, was the museum's curator, so young Rudyard knew the spot well.

n.certNote: The facts of who wrote what are clear. How to judge these writers is debated. Some readers value their stories and their love of India's landscapes, while others point out that many of them supported the British Empire and saw India through its eyes.

sec.t:
Kipling spent his early childhood in Bombay, speaking Hindustani with his servants before English. He later returned to India as a young [[@journalism|journalist]] in Lahore. His stories, such as *Plain Tales from the Hills* and [[@jungle-book|The Jungle Book]], made him famous. In 1907 he became the first English-language writer to win the Nobel Prize in Literature.

His novel *Kim*, published in 1901, follows an orphan boy who wanders the Grand Trunk Road with a Tibetan lama. Many readers find it full of affection for India's crowds, colours and languages.

But Kipling also strongly supported the British Empire. His poem "The White Man's Burden" (1899) argued that Western countries had a duty to rule other peoples. Many readers, then and now, have criticised these views. George Orwell, who admired some of his writing, called him an imperialist.

{{story:east-india-company}}

E. M. Forster visited India in the 1910s and 1920s and wrote *A Passage to India* (1924). It shows friendships between Indians and British people breaking down under the unfairness of [[colonial|colonial]] rule, and many saw it as critical of the Raj.

George Orwell was born Eric Blair in 1903 in Motihari, Bihar, where his father worked for the colonial government. He left as a baby, but later served in the British police in Burma, and grew to dislike [[empire|empire]] deeply.

Jim Corbett, born in Nainital in what is now [[@uttarakhand|Uttarakhand]], wrote *Man-Eaters of Kumaon* (1944) about tracking tigers and leopards that attacked villagers. He later worked to protect wildlife, and India's first national park was renamed Corbett National Park after him in 1956.

In 1978, the scholar Edward Said published *Orientalism*. He argued that many Western writers described Asia as mysterious and backward, partly to justify ruling it. His ideas changed how many people read Kipling and his circle.

Indian writers had been answering back in English for years. [[@rk-narayan|R. K. Narayan]], Mulk Raj Anand and Raja Rao, all publishing in the 1930s, wrote about Indian life from the inside, with ordinary people as heroes instead of servants or backdrops.

Some British families never left. Ruskin Bond was born in Kasauli in 1934 to a British family. After a few years in England as a young man, he came back and made India his home. He has spent his life writing about the hills of Mussoorie and the people who live there, and many Indian readers see him simply as one of their own.

That may be the clearest change since Kipling's day. Writing about India in English is no longer mainly done by visitors. Today, most of it is written by [[@indian-english-writers|Indian writers]] themselves.

text: Gurmukhi is the [[script|script]] used to write Punjabi in India. Its name means "from the mouth of the Guru". It was shaped and spread in the 1500s by Guru Angad Dev, the second of the ten [[@sikh-gurus|Sikh Gurus]]. He wanted ordinary people to be able to read and write the hymns of [[@guru-nanak|Guru Nanak]].

Gurmukhi has 35 letters in its [[@words-alphabet-order|traditional order]], written left to right, hanging from a line along the top. It is used for everyday Punjabi in newspapers, shop signs and schoolbooks, and for the [[@guru-granth-sahib|Guru Granth Sahib]], the holy book of Sikhism.

st.reveal: In Pakistan, Punjabi is usually written in Shahmukhi, which runs right to left like Urdu. In India, it is written in Gurmukhi, which runs left to right. The spoken language is largely the same on both sides.

sec.t:
Before Gurmukhi became widespread, Punjabi had no single standard script. Merchants used quick shorthand scripts for their accounts, and learned people often wrote in Sanskrit or Persian.

Guru Angad Dev took letters already in use in the region, arranged them clearly and taught them widely. Learning to read Gurmukhi became part of growing up Sikh. It is often said that the Guru taught children their letters himself, though stories like this are hard to check. When Guru Arjan Dev, the fifth Guru, compiled the hymns of the Gurus and other saints into the Adi Granth in 1604, he wrote it in Gurmukhi. That holy book, later called the Guru Granth Sahib, is still kept in every gurdwara, including the Golden Temple in [[@amritsar|Amritsar]].

Like most Indian scripts, Gurmukhi is an [[abugida|abugida]]. Each consonant has a built-in "a" sound, and small marks above, below or beside a letter change the vowel.

{{story:sikh-gurus}}

When India was divided in 1947, the Punjab region was cut in two. [[@partition|Partition]] left the western half in Pakistan and the eastern half in India. Millions of people were forced to move across the new border.

Punjabi did not split, but its writing did. In Pakistan, Punjabi is usually written in Shahmukhi, a script based on [[@arabic-script|Perso-Arabic]] letters that runs right to left. India's 2011 Census counted about 3.3 crore Punjabi speakers, but Pakistan has far more, so most of the world's Punjabi speakers do not write in Gurmukhi at all.

A poem by the 18th-century Sufi poet Bulleh Shah or by Waris Shah, who wrote the love story *Heer Ranjha*, is loved on both sides of the border. It just looks different on the page.

Punjabi has a rare feature for a North Indian language: tones. Like Chinese, it can change a word's meaning through the rise or fall of your voice. Words that look almost the same written down may sound different when spoken.

This happened as certain sounds that older forms of the language once had, like a breathy "gh" or "bh", slowly faded and left a change of pitch in their place. Gurmukhi still writes those old letters, so a reader has to know that a letter like ਘ now often signals a tone, not a breathy sound.

Punjabi speakers have spread far. Many Punjabi families settled in Canada, the UK and the USA from the 20th century onwards. In Canada, Punjabi is one of the most spoken languages after English and French, and there are Punjabi street signs in parts of Vancouver and Toronto.

The beats of [[@bhangra|bhangra]], once a harvest dance in Punjab's villages, now fill dance floors in London and New York. Many young Punjabis abroad learn Gurmukhi on weekends at their local gurdwara, so they can read the same hymns their great-grandparents read.

text: The Ramayana is one of India's two great [[epic|epics]], long poems about heroes and gods. It tells the story of Rama, a prince of Ayodhya, who is sent into the forest for 14 years. His wife Sita and his brother Lakshmana go with him. Ravana, the ten-headed king of Lanka, carries Sita away. With the help of Hanuman and an army of monkeys and bears, Rama builds a bridge across the sea, defeats Ravana and brings Sita home.
The oldest known version is in [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]] and is traditionally said to be by the sage Valmiki. For many Hindus, Rama is a form of the god Vishnu, and the story is sacred.

st.reveal: The Ramakien is Thailand's national epic, a retelling of the Ramayana. Scenes from it are painted around the walls of the Temple of the Emerald Buddha in Bangkok.

n.certNote: Scholars date Valmiki's Ramayana to roughly 2,000 to 2,500 years ago, but estimates vary. For many Hindus the story is sacred and its events are history. Historians study it as an ancient epic.

sec.t:
Valmiki's Ramayana has about 24,000 verses, divided into seven books called *kandas*. Scholars disagree about its date. Many think it took shape over several centuries, starting somewhere between about 500 and 300 BCE, with the first and last books probably added later. Tradition calls Valmiki the *adikavi*, the first poet.

A famous story tells how his poetry began. Valmiki saw a hunter shoot one of a pair of birds. His grief poured out in a new verse form, the *shloka*, the [[@rhythm-beat|rhythm]] in which most of the Ramayana is written. The story is told in the Ramayana itself, so it is a legend about the poem's own birth.

The story travelled with traders and priests to Southeast Asia more than 1,000 years ago. In [[@thailand|Thailand]] it became the *Ramakien*, and [[mural|murals]] of it run around the walls of the Temple of the Emerald Buddha in Bangkok. In Cambodia it is the *Reamker*, and long stone carvings of the great battle cover a gallery wall at [[@angkor-wat|Angkor Wat]]. On the [[@bali|island of Bali]], where most people are Hindu, it is performed in dance.

Shadow [[@puppetry|puppet]] plays of the Ramayana are performed in Indonesia, Malaysia, Kerala and Karnataka. In Indonesia, a Muslim-majority country, a Ramayana [[@ballet|ballet]] is still staged in the open air beside the Prambanan temple in Java.

sec.h: Alive in homes and on screens
sec.t:
In north India, Ramlila performances act out the story each year in the days before Dussehra, which celebrates Rama's victory over Ravana. Many people link Diwali with Rama's return to Ayodhya, when lamps were lit to welcome him home.

In 1987, Ramanand Sagar's *Ramayan* began on Doordarshan, India's national [[@tv-india|TV channel]]. On Sunday mornings, streets emptied as families gathered around [[@television-invented|television]] sets, sometimes the only one in the neighbourhood. When the series was shown again during the 2020 lockdown, it drew huge audiences once more. A story first sung by poets in Sanskrit had found new listeners on screens, more than two thousand years later.

text: Bubblegum is pink mostly because of an accident of history. In 1928, a young accountant named Walter Diemer was working at the Fleer chewing gum company in Philadelphia. In his spare time, he experimented with gum recipes, trying to make one that would stretch into bubbles without sticking to everything.
When he finally got a batch that worked, he needed to colour it. According to Diemer, the only food colouring in the factory was pink. So pink it was.
His gum, called Dubble Bubble, sold out fast. Other companies copied the recipe and the colour. Within a few years, "bubblegum pink" was a colour of its own.

sec.h: The quest for the perfect bubble
sec.t:
Gum that blows bubbles needs to be stretchy but not too sticky. Frank Fleer, who started the company, had tried before, in 1906. His gum, Blibber-Blubber, stretched but stuck to faces and was hard to wash off.

Diemer tried batch after batch. He later said he wasn't a chemist and had no idea what he was doing. Then one day in 1928, a batch came out right: stretchy, strong and much less sticky.

The company sold Dubble Bubble for a cent a piece. Diemer is said to have taught shop staff how to blow bubbles, so they could show children. He never got rich from it, but he was proud of the gum for the rest of his life. Pink stayed the classic colour even after other brands tried green, blue and purple.

{{story:accident-vulcanised-rubber}}

Early chewing gum was made from chicle, a milky sap from the sapodilla tree of Mexico and Central America. The [[@aztecs-maya|Maya and Aztecs]] chewed chicle more than a thousand years ago.

Today most gum base is made from synthetic [[polymer|polymers]]. These are long, chain-like [[molecule|molecules]], similar to those in some plastics and rubbers. One of them, polyisobutylene, is also used in the inner tubes of [[@tyres|tyres]]. It sounds alarming, but food-grade versions are tested for safety.

The base is mixed with sugar or sweeteners, softeners and flavours, a recipe unpacked in [[@chewing-gum|what chewing gum is made of]]. Gum makers test how long the flavour lasts and how the gum feels after an hour of chewing.

Bubblegum flavour is not one fruit. It is a mix, and each company keeps its recipe secret. It often includes fruity notes of banana, strawberry, cherry or pineapple, sometimes with a hint of wintergreen or cinnamon.

The colour may help our brains taste it. Many people link pink with sweetness and fruit, a connection explored in [[@colour-meaning|what colours mean]].

The pink in modern gum comes from food colourings. In January 2025, the US Food and Drug Administration banned one of them, called Red No. 3, from food, giving companies until 2027 to remove it. Many gum makers use other colours instead.

People have chewed things for a long time. [[archaeologist|Archaeologists]] in Denmark found a lump of chewed birch tar about 5,700 years old, with tooth marks and DNA from the person who chewed it.

But gum can be a nuisance. Old gum sticks to pavements and is costly to scrape off. In 1992, [[@singapore|Singapore]] banned the sale of chewing gum, partly after people stuck it on the doors of its new metro trains, stopping them from closing. Since 2004, gum that helps people quit smoking or protects teeth can be sold there by pharmacists.

And the strangest part? The rubbery stretch that lets gum blow bubbles comes from the same family of materials as car tyres, which got their strength from a lucky kitchen accident in the 1800s.

text: Northeast India is eight states and hundreds of communities, so there's no single "Northeast food". But many kitchens share some habits. Rice is [[@grains-world|the main grain]]. Food is often boiled, steamed or smoked rather than fried, and many dishes use very little oil and few dry spices.

Flavour comes from fresh herbs, [[@bamboo|bamboo]] shoots, fermented foods and fierce local chillies, including the bhut jolokia, once named the hottest chilli in the world. Pork, fish and chicken are common in many communities, while others, especially in Assam's plains, eat lots of fish and vegetables.

The eight northeastern states have dozens of communities with very different cuisines. Momos are popular in Sikkim and nearby hills, but Assamese, Naga, Manipuri, Mizo, Khasi and Tripuri food each have their own dishes and flavours.

sec.t:
[[@fermentation|Fermentation]] is at the heart of many northeastern kitchens. [[microbe|Microbes]] slowly change the food, adding deep, strong flavours and helping it keep.

In Nagaland, axone (also spelt akhuni) is [[@soybeans|fermented soybean]] with a powerful smell. Manipur's ngari is fermented fish, used in chutneys and stews. Khasi cooks in [[@meghalaya|Meghalaya]] make tungrymbai, another fermented soybean dish. Fermented bamboo shoots add sourness to curries across the region. In Sikkim, gundruk is made from fermented leafy greens, dried and used in soups.

The bhut jolokia, or ghost pepper, grows in Assam, Nagaland and Manipur. In 2007, Guinness World Records named it the world's hottest chilli. Hotter chillies have since been bred elsewhere, but it's still one of the [[@spicy-hot|spiciest]] in the world.

People in the region use it carefully, often in a fiery chutney, pounded with tomatoes or fermented fish. Cooks sometimes wear gloves when handling it, because its juice can sting the skin and eyes. Even a small piece can make a whole pot of curry hot.

Assamese food is gentler. A favourite is masor tenga, a light, sour fish curry flavoured with tomato or lemon. Many meals start with khar, a dish made with an alkaline liquid filtered through the ash of dried banana peels.

Assam is also famous for its tea. Its strong black tea is drunk across India and exported around the world. Rural Assamese families still make jolpan, a breakfast of flattened or puffed rice with curd and [[@jaggery|jaggery]].

In Sikkim and the hills near Darjeeling, Tibetan and Nepali influences are strong. [[@food-momos|Momos]], steamed dumplings stuffed with vegetables or meat, and thukpa, a noodle soup, are everyday foods. Momos are now sold at street stalls across Indian cities, from [[@shillong|Shillong]] to Bengaluru.

Sikkim's farms became fully organic in 2016, and its fresh greens, mushrooms and herbs go into simple soups and stir-fries. For many travellers, a plate of northeastern food is a first taste of how different Indian cooking can be from one end of the country to the other.
